analysis.one_liner: Cuts individual and corporate tax rates, repeals the alternative minimum tax, and pays for it by ending many deductions and credits.
analysis.headline: A 968-page rewrite of the tax code introduced by the House's tax-committee chairman in December 2014 drew zero cosponsors, never received a committee markup, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the seven current income tax brackets with three lower ones (10%, 25%, and 35%), repealed the alternative minimum tax, and cut the corporate rate from 35% to 25%. To pay for it, the bill repealed or trimmed a long list of tax breaks used by both families and businesses — including deductions for medical expenses, moving expenses, student loan interest, and the child care and adoption credits, as well as business breaks like last-in-first-out accounting and like-kind exchanges. It would also have exempted 95% of foreign profits of U.S. multinational corporations from U.S. tax, capped the mortgage interest deduction at $500,000 of debt, and imposed a new tax on the largest banks and a limit on executive compensation.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly every income group would have seen a lower marginal rate, and middle-income families would have gained from a roughly doubled standard deduction and a larger child tax credit. The largest gains, though, went to investors and corporations: capital gains and qualified dividends would have been taxed at an effective rate of about 21% (a 40% deduction from gross income on top of the new 35% top rate), the corporate rate would have dropped to 25%, and multinationals would have gained a near-exemption on foreign earnings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families broadly, plus investors and corporations

how_it_helps.text: Replaces seven individual tax brackets with three — 10%, 25%, and 35% — and adds a 5-percentage-point surcharge only above roughly $400,000 of income for most filers.
Sets a single standard deduction of $22,000 for married couples and $11,000 for singles, with an extra $5,500 deduction for single parents, and increases the child tax credit.
Repeals the alternative minimum tax, a parallel system that forces millions of households to compute their taxes twice.
Cuts the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25% beginning in 2019, offset by repealing dozens of corporate deductions and credits rather than by adding to the deficit.
Creates a one-time transition to exempt 95% of foreign dividends paid to U.S. multinational parents, moving the U.S. to a territorial-style system of taxing foreign income.

Curbs executive pay by tightening the $1 million deduction limit and imposing a 25% excise tax on compensation above $1 million at tax-exempt organizations, and imposes a 0.035% quarterly surtax on financial institutions with over $500 billion in assets.
Repeals the medical device excise tax and expands the exemption from the branded prescription drug fee to rare-disease drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Households that use the repealed breaks — the deductions for medical expenses, moving expenses, student loan interest, and alimony, and the credits for child care, adoption, and first-time home purchases — and anyone with over $500,000 of mortgage debt or planning a traditional IRA contribution, which the bill bars. On the business side, large banks, oil and gas producers, real estate investors, life insurers, and tax-exempt institutions like private universities would have borne the offsets that finance the rate cuts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Break users, large banks, oil, real estate, universities

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the deduction for medical expenses and the credits for employment-related child care and adoption expenses, and repeals the student loan interest deduction — tax provisions used mostly by middle-income and modest-income households — while cutting the top rate.

It caps the mortgage interest deduction at interest on $500,000 of acquisition debt, down from $1 million, and tightens the exclusion for gain on home sales to five of the prior eight years and once every five years.
It prohibits new contributions to traditional IRAs and bars employers from creating new SIMPLE 401(k) plans, eliminating some retirement savings channels.
The bill repeals the low-income housing tax credit, the work opportunity tax credit, and the small-employer pension startup credit, tools aimed at affordable housing and hiring disadvantaged workers.

The transition to exempting foreign earnings lets corporations bring back profits accumulated offshore under a reduced rate, a step that independent estimates at the time projected would shift revenue toward shareholders of multinationals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a genuine trade rather than a giveaway: it cut rates and simplified filing for nearly everyone, and it paid for those cuts with real repeals that hit industries and high earners hard. But the distribution was uneven — the biggest structural gains (the capital gains deduction, the 25% corporate rate, the foreign-profits exemption) accrue to shareholders and multinationals, while many of the repealed breaks were worth modest amounts to middle-income families. It also paired tax increases on the biggest banks with a repeal of the medical device tax, protecting one health-sector industry while taxing another. As a comprehensive reform it was more honest than most about paying for itself, but families that rely on the repealed credits would have come out behind the families that itemize large gains.

outcome.mechanism: The chairman of the House tax-writing committee released this bill with three weeks left in the session; it was referred to his own committee, never marked up, never scheduled for a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI), chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on December 10, 2014, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the same day.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
Camp delivered introductory remarks on the bill on December 12, 2014; that was the last recorded action before the session ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill was the product of a year-long drafting process in which Camp had released successive discussion drafts of each section of the tax code, but his committee never took up the finished bill.
Because the bill never received a markup, hearing, or vote, no member's position on it was ever recorded in a roll call.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, wealthy households, large banks, and oil and gas interests are better off because the bill died — the existing tax code's rates and preferences, including the 39.6% top rate's accompanying 23.8% capital gains rate and the deductions the bill would have repealed, all stayed in place. Middle-income families kept the credits the bill would have scrapped, but kept the higher rates and complexity too.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies and wealthy taxpayers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Dave Camp
for.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the comprehensive tax reform bill on December 10, 2014 and delivered introductory remarks on it two days later.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee staff and the drafting coalition around Chairman Camp
for.what_they_did: Assembled a roughly 968-page rewrite covering individual, corporate, international, and tax-exempt taxation over Camp's two-year chairmanship, released in full text on introduction.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or a floor vote during the three remaining weeks of the session.

against.name: Business and industry lobbying groups
against.role: Financial, retail, energy, real estate, and insurance lobbies
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill's offsets, including the surtax on large banks, the repeal of LIFO accounting, and the rollback of real estate and insurance preferences, in the weeks after its release.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Did not endorse the proposal and signaled the administration would not push it in the remaining session.

against.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
against.role: Incoming Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee (2015)
against.what_they_did: Took over the committee the following month and pursued a different, narrower tax agenda rather than advancing Camp's bill.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party signed on and no markup or roll call ever occurred, so the partisan split on the bill was never recorded — it sat as a chairman's proposal that neither party moved.

industries.note: The bill would exempt 95% of foreign dividends paid to U.S. corporate parents and impose only a one-time reduced-rate toll on accumulated offshore profits, permanently lowering tax on foreign earnings. That shifts the tax base away from multinational shareholders and toward domestic-only taxpayers.

Institutions with over $500 billion in assets would pay a new quarterly 0.035% excise tax and face limits on FDIC premium deductions and reinsurance with untaxed affiliates. Smaller financial firms would gain from the lower corporate rate.

The bill repeals percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, marginal well credits, and special rules for gain on coal and iron, while extending the per-barrel oil spill tax and expanding the 'crude oil' excise base to tar sands and oil shale. Some of that excise increase passes through to consumers at the pump.

The bill caps mortgage interest deductions at $500,000 of debt, repeals like-kind exchanges for property, tightens the home-sale exclusion, and repeals the first-time homebuyer credit, while keeping REITs as pass-through entities with modified rules.
The bill repeals the Affordable Care Act's 2.3% excise tax on medical devices, removing a revenue source that helped fund health coverage expansion.
The bill exempts rare-disease drugs from the annual fee on branded prescription drug sales and repeals the clinical testing credit for orphan drugs, while keeping the rest of the branded-drug fee.

The bill subjects more tax-exempt entities to the unrelated business income tax, imposes a 1% excise tax on net investment income of private colleges and universities, repeals the tax exemption for professional sports leagues and co-op health insurers, and restricts donor disclosure rules for social welfare organizations.

The bill repeals the small life insurance company deduction, modifies reserve and proration rules, repeals the special treatment of Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations, and bars deductions for reinsurance premiums paid to untaxed foreign affiliates.
